newsitem.title: UK: Argentine economy to overcome job blues - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Argentine economy to overcome job blues - analysts.

text.p: Argentine unemployment remains high but is not seen as a stumbling block for the country's surging economy, analysts said on Monday.
"In general, there is a feeling of bullishness," said Peter West, chief economist at BBV Latinvest.
Argentina's Economy Ministry on Friday reported a drop in unemployment to 16.1 percent of the workforce in May from 17.3 percent at the time of the last twice-yearly jobs survey in October.
The jobless rate has risen from just seven percent when President Carlos Menem took office in 1989 and hit a peak of 18.4 percent during the recession of 1995.
But London analysts were not concerned that the slow decline in unemployment would derail the country's rapid growth prospects.
In fact, Santander Investment has joined the ranks of banks that have upgraded their Argentine growth forecasts, upping its 1997 growth estimate to 7.3 percent from 5.5 percent.
"Our 7.3 percent forecast for 1997 makes Argentina the fastest-growing economy of the big seven Latin American countries and places it among the top five economies worldwide," Santander said.
Analysts said the lack of a sharper decline in unemployment might reduce the prospects of Menem's government in October's mid-term Congressional elections.
However, that could strengthen the president's determination to press ahead with labour market reforms before his mandate runs out in 1999.
"The unions are never going to win this one," said Richard Gray, senior emerging markets analyst at Bank of America, referring to confrontation between unions and the president on laboor reforms.
"They (the unions) are on a loser. They would be taking on convertibility," if they stopped Menem from introducing labour reforms, said Gray.

The government and many economists argue that reforming the labour market is crucial for cutting the high costs to businesses of hiring and firing, which are seen as the biggest obstacle to increasing employment.

Such labour market changes would be a natural continuation of Argentina's reform process, which started with the introduction in 1991 of convertibility, pegging the value of the peso to the dollar at par, analysts said.

The government decreed new labour laws last year but they were challenged by the courts as unconstitutional. It then agreed on a less ambitious package of reforms which have been sent to Congress for approval.
"I think people here are following market reforms very closely," said West.
Friday's report signalled that the country's accelerating growth was feeding through to the job market with or without labour market reforms.
According to the report, the economy created a total of 518,000 jobs in the year to end-May 1997 and 320,000 jobs since October.
"This is the largest growth in employment since 1980, the year in which the figure began to be measured," the economy ministry's chief advisor, Carlos Rodriguez, said.
"The most encouraging fact (of the report) was job creation," said West.
